bib.title: Chapter 10: On-policy Control with Approximation (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)
bib.venue: MIT Press (book chapter, pp. 244-256; authors inferred from the book, not printed in the chapter)

question: How do semi-gradient TD methods extend from state-value prediction to on-policy control with parametric action-value approximation, and how must the continuing-task objective change?
contributions: Episodic semi-gradient one-step and n-step Sarsa with linear tile-coded q-hat, demonstrated on Mountain Car
Average-reward setting with differential returns, value functions and TD errors, and differential semi-gradient (n-step) Sarsa
An argument that discounting has no role in defining the continuing control problem under function approximation

results.claim: Under function approximation, the average of discounted returns equals r(pi)/(1-gamma), so gamma does not change the ordering of policies and discounting is futile for defining continuing control.
results.setup: Continuing tasks, objective J(pi) = sum of mu_pi(s) v^gamma_pi(s), ergodic MDP; proof in the box on p. 254
results.quote: returns is proportional to the average reward

results.claim: Differential semi-gradient Sarsa on the 10-server access-control queue learned an average reward estimate of about 2.31.
results.setup: Tabular, 10 servers, customers priority 1/2/4/8, busy server frees with p = 0.06, alpha = 0.01, beta = 0.01, epsilon = 0.1, initial values and R-bar zero, after 2 million steps, one run

results.claim: n-step semi-gradient Sarsa learns faster and reaches better asymptotic performance at n=8 than n=1 on Mountain Car.
results.setup: Mountain Car, 8 tilings tile coding, epsilon-greedy, averaged over 100 runs; alpha = 0.5/8 for n=1 and 0.3/8 for n=8 (Fig 10.3)
results.quote: performance is best if an intermediate level of bootstrapping

results.claim: Intermediate bootstrapping (n = 4) gave the best early performance among n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
results.setup: Mountain Car, tile coding with 8 tilings, steps per episode averaged over first 50 episodes and 100 runs, selected alpha values; standard errors from 0.5 (n=1) to about 4 (n=16)
results.quote: an intermediate level of bootstrapping (n = 4) performed best

results.claim: Mountain Car tile coding used 8 tilings, each tile covering 1/8th of the bounded range per dimension.
results.setup: Mountain Car, tiles3 with iht=IHT(4096), linear q-hat = w^T x(s,a)
results.quote: 8 tilings, with each tile covering 1/8th of the bounded distance in each dimension

results.claim: Optimistic zero initial action values caused extensive exploration even with epsilon = 0 on Mountain Car.
results.setup: Mountain Car single run, all true values negative, reward -1 per step

results.claim: Linear semi-gradient Sarsa with epsilon-greedy does not converge in the usual sense but enters a bounded region near the best solution.
results.quote: does not converge in the usual sense, but does enter a bounded region near

results.claim: With function approximation the policy improvement theorem is lost, so no local improvement guarantee exists for action-value methods; epsilon-greedification can yield a worse policy as policies chatter.
results.setup: General statement, cites Gordon (1996a); policy-gradient theorem (ch. 13) plays the corresponding role
results.quote: we have lost the policy improvement theorem

results.claim: Differential semi-gradient Sarsa converges to differential values plus an arbitrary offset.
results.setup: Average-reward setting; offset does not affect Bellman equations or TD errors

limits: Episodic Mountain Car results are linear tile coding only, averaged over 100 runs; no deep networks.
Continuous or large discrete action sets are called an open research topic with no clear resolution.
Differential Sarsa has an arbitrary-offset limitation; removing it is left as future research.
Access-control example is tabular, a single run, and the authors note the drop at high free-server counts is probably insufficient data.
Fig 10.1 data came from semi-gradient Sarsa(lambda), not plain Sarsa (footnote 2).
Chapter covers on-policy only; off-policy and the deadly triad are in ch. 11 (not in this extract).
practices: Use n-step returns with intermediate n (about 4 to 8) as the update target for semi-gradient Sarsa (10.2, Fig 10.4).
For discrete, small action sets, take argmax of q-hat over actions and use an epsilon-greedy policy for on-policy improvement (10.1).
For continuing tasks with function approximation, use the average-reward objective with differential values rather than discounting (10.3-10.4).
Update the average-reward estimate with the TD error delta rather than R - R-bar, which is more stable (Ex 10.8, 10.5 pseudocode).
Use a small beta for the average-reward step size, or the unbiased constant-step-size trick (Ex 10.9).
Optimistic initial values can drive exploration without epsilon in tasks with negative rewards (Example 10.1).
